problem: The lead says the three measured variables 'set the acid–base state', but pO₂ does not take part in acid–base balance; it reports oxygenation. A student may think a low pO₂ makes blood acidic.
fix: A blood gas analyser measures three variables in arterial blood: pH, pCO₂ and pO₂. pH and pCO₂ (with the calculated bicarbonate) set the acid–base state; pO₂ shows how well the lungs load oxygen.

problem: The chamber is held at 37 °C and the sample warms to that temperature inside it, so a cold sample measured there does not give a 'falsely low pCO₂ and falsely high pH'. The lower pCO₂ and higher pH belong to a sample measured below 37 °C (CO₂ solubility rises, electrode slope changes). As written, the stated cause and the stated effect do not match the setup.
fix: The chamber is held at 37 °C because the electrodes are calibrated there and the blood equilibria are defined there. A sample measured below 37 °C reads a lower pCO₂ and a higher pH, because CO₂ solubility rises and the electrode slope changes; a sample warmed in the 37 °C chamber gives 37 °C values, which still need correcting to the patient's own body temperature.

problem: The sentence says co-oximetry measures 'haemoglobin species, electrolytes and lactate'. Co-oximetry measures haemoglobin species only; electrolytes and lactate come from separate ion-selective and amperometric sensors on the cartridge.
fix: Modern analysers add co-oximetry for haemoglobin species, plus thick-film ion-selective and amperometric sensors for electrolytes and lactate on the same cartridge.
